records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Purpose and isolation model FortiGate VRFs create separate routing tables. A route learned in VRF 10 is not automatically visible in VRF 20, even when both VRFs live in the same VDOM. Route leaking is an explicit control-plane operation that copies selected reachability between routing instances. It does not merge the routing tables, bypass firewall policy, or make every interface mutually reachable. Objects and transaction flow The documented BGP example uses a hub with branch prefixes learned into separate VRFs. A pair of virtual inter-VDOM-link interfaces forms the logical handoff. Although an inter-VDOM link normally joins VDOMs, FortiOS can use two ends in the same VDOM with different VRF assignments. Each end receives an address and a VRF ID. Prefix lists define which networks are eligible; route maps bind those lists to the leak; BGP leak-target entries identify the destination VRF and transit interface. The return direction needs its own leak-target and route map. A one-way leak may install a route but still leave replies without a route. Fortinet’s example enables subnet overlap when the interface design requires it, creates the VDOM link, assigns the two interface endpoints to VRF 10 and VRF 20, defines prefix lists and route maps, then configures the BGP VRF leak targets. The core relationship is source VRF → route map → destination VRF over the selected link. Keep the prefixes narrow; a broad prefix list can accidentally expose management or tenant networks. config system global set single-vdom-npuvlink enable end config router bgp config vrf edit 10 config leak-target edit 20 set route-map "Leak_from_VRF10_to_VRF20" set interface "link-10-20-0" next end next end end The NPU-link setting is an optional acceleration path on supported models; it does not create the route leak by itself. The Fortinet guide also requires a firewall policy that permits the inter-VRF traffic. A route in the destination table is therefore necessary but not sufficient for packet delivery. Evidence and troubleshooting Inspect the source VRF first: the expected BGP prefix must exist and be active. Then inspect the prefix-list match, route-map rule, BGP leak-target destination, and transit interface assignment. Check the destination VRF routing table for the leaked prefix and verify the reverse prefix is present in the opposite direction. Finally inspect the firewall policy counters and capture both sides of the link. A route-table entry proves control-plane reachability; it does not prove the policy allows the packet or that the return path exists. If the route is present but traffic fails, do not keep changing BGP timers. Check the inter-VRF firewall policy, source/destination interface selection, overlapping subnet assumptions, and reverse leak. If the route is absent, isolate the failure before the data plane: BGP learning, prefix-list match, route-map, leak-target, then link/VRF binding. records.lesson_subject: Workflow mode as an ADOM change transaction: session isolation, ordered approval, rejection cascades, and separate device installation
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: workflow-mode-as-an-adom-change-transaction-session-isolation-ordered-approval-rejection-cascades-and-separate-device-installation
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Why workflow mode exists FortiManager workflow mode makes an ADOM change a reviewable transaction instead of allowing administrators to edit the shared database directly. It is intended for environments where policy and object changes require a submitter, one or more approval groups, and an auditable decision before changes are committed to the ADOM. This differs from ordinary workspace locking: workspace mode prevents concurrent edits by locking an ADOM, device, or policy package; workflow mode records a session with a change set and approval state. Session lifecycle Workflow approvals must be configured for the ADOM before a session can be created. The ADOM is locked, a session is started, and policy/object changes are made inside that session. The session list tracks the transaction. View Diff compares the proposed change set with the ADOM baseline; it can be inspected without locking the ADOM. A session can be saved and continued later, submitted for approval, or discarded. A saved session blocks creation of another new session until it is submitted or discarded. Approval is ordered. Sessions are approved in the order they were created, and each configured approval group must satisfy its approval requirement. A rejection blocks later sessions from advancing until the rejected session is repaired/resubmitted or discarded. Discarding a session also discards all later sessions, because those later change sets were built on a sequence that no longer exists. Reverting to an earlier approved session creates a new rollback transaction; it is not an invisible edit of history. Per-ADOM workspace mode lets one ADOM use Workflow while another uses Workspace or Disable. Fortinet documents set workspace-mode per-adom for enabling per-ADOM selection and set workspace-mode workflow for workflow mode across all ADOMs. Changing workspace mode ends the current GUI session and requires a new login. In workflow mode, Device Manager and Policy & Objects are read-only outside an active workflow session. Approval is not the device install Approval commits the approved changes into FortiManager’s ADOM configuration workflow. It does not prove the target FortiGate has received the configuration. After approval, use the Install Wizard, select the intended policy package and device settings, review the install preview, and run the installation. Verify the task history and the device’s configuration/policy-package status separately. Operational evidence For a stalled change, inspect the ADOM’s workflow mode, approval matrix, session state, creator, creation order, and View Diff. A submitted session awaiting approval is not an install failure. A fully approved session with an out-of-date FortiGate points to the separate install stage. If the modifier/approver identity is wrong or appears as a generic account, compare the FortiManager release with known issues before altering the approval matrix. Preserve the session log and diff; do not discard an earlier session casually because later queued sessions can be removed with it.

records.lesson_subject: Report dataset execution: Log Type binding, $log/$filter expansion, query analysis, hcache, and test-result boundaries
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: report-dataset-execution-log-type-binding-log-filter-expansion-query-analysis-hcache-and-test-result-boundaries
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Dataset is the report’s query contract A FortiAnalyzer dataset is a named query over log data. Charts and report macros reference the dataset; when a report runs, the dataset supplies the rows used to render those components. The dataset’s Log Type is not a cosmetic label: it selects the underlying log family/table that the query’s $log macro represents. A query written for Traffic logs cannot be assumed to work unchanged against Event, UTM, or Local Event data because the columns and semantics differ. Execution pipeline In an ADOM deployment, first select the correct ADOM. Create the dataset under Reports → Report Definitions → Datasets, choose the Log Type, and write SQL against $log . Fortinet’s examples use $filter in the WHERE clause so the report time-range filter is injected into the query. If it is omitted, a report can ignore the user-selected time window or produce misleading results. A compact traffic example is: SELECT from_itime(itime)::date AS day, SUM(rcvdbyte) AS inbound, SUM(sentbyte) AS outbound, policyid, devid FROM $log WHERE $filter GROUP BY day, policyid, devid ORDER BY day Use Validate to catch SQL syntax/field errors. Analyze Query is more diagnostic: it shows the original query, any transformed query, validation results, and the hcache query when auto-cache is enabled. The transformed query matters because the report engine may rewrite a dataset for chart/report context. A query that validates is not necessarily performant at production scale. Variables can expose expressions as report filter fields. For example, a User variable can normalize a username and fall back to the source IP. This creates a stable report filter even when the raw logs have inconsistent user fields. Test lets the administrator choose a time period and devices/VDOMs before saving. The Community SQL guidance notes that test output is a sample rather than a full report result; treat it as query validation, not a complete volume audit. Failure isolation If the dataset returns no rows, verify the ADOM, Log Type, selected devices, time window, and whether the relevant FortiGate policies actually logged the events. If the query validates but the report is empty, inspect the report-level device filter and chart-level filters. If a chart’s Order By is enabled, it can override the dataset’s ORDER BY clause. For local-event datasets, verify the source is available in the correct ADOM and that local-event retention covers the requested interval. Use predefined datasets as the starting point where possible; Fortinet optimizes them for its report engine and hcache behavior. A custom query should be tested with a narrow period, analyzed for its transformed form, and then exercised against representative devices before being placed in a scheduled report. A successful Test proves the sample query ran; it does not prove the report’s final filters, full time span, or cache plan are correct.

records.lesson_subject: MAB Access-Request integrity: Message-Authenticator, call-check semantics, and RADIUS server compatibility
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: mab-access-request-integrity-message-authenticator-call-check-semantics-and-radius-server-compatibility
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: MAB is a RADIUS identity exchange, not 802.1X MAC Authentication Bypass is used when an endpoint cannot run an 802.1X supplicant. The FortiSwitch acts as the NAS and sends a RADIUS Access-Request using the endpoint MAC address as the identity. FortiSwitchOS documents the MAB request attributes: NAS-Identifier, User-Name, User-Password, Service-Type, NAS-Port-Id, NAS-Port, NAS-Port-Type, Calling-Station-ID, Framed-MTU, and Message-Authenticator. For MAB, Service-Type is always call-check , regardless of the configured Service-Type setting. This differs from an 802.1X request, which carries EAP-Message and the EAP exchange. Why Message-Authenticator matters FortiSwitchOS 7.0.8 introduced Message-Authenticator in MAB Access-Request messages. Attribute 80 authenticates the entire RADIUS packet using the shared secret; it is not simply a field containing the endpoint MAC. The server must validate the attribute and the same RADIUS shared secret must be configured on both sides. A server policy or older RADIUS implementation that assumes a legacy MAB request shape can reject the packet even though the MAC identity and NAS-Port are correct. When comparing a working and failing switch, inspect the actual Access-Request. Confirm the username/calling-station ID format, NAS-Identifier, NAS-Port-Id, Service-Type=call-check, and Message-Authenticator presence/validation. The Community MAC-format tip shows that username, password, and calling-station delimiters can be changed (hyphen, colon, or none; upper/lower case). That is a separate interoperability variable from Message-Authenticator. A matching MAC string does not prove packet integrity validation passed. Operational troubleshooting Start with the switch’s RADIUS server definition and shared secret, then capture the request at the server. Determine whether the request reaches the server, whether the server rejects integrity validation, whether the policy matches the NAS/client identity, and whether the response returns to the switch. Compare MAB with a known-good 802.1X request: the MAB request uses the call-check service type and MAC identity, while 802.1X carries EAP payloads. Do not diagnose every Access-Reject as a bad endpoint MAC. On a firmware upgrade, confirm the target FortiSwitch model and FortiSwitchOS feature support before changing the RADIUS policy. A new Message-Authenticator field can expose a server-side compatibility or shared-secret problem that did not appear with the older request format. If the server rejects the packet, fix its RADIUS validation/client policy; changing VLAN assignment on the switch will not repair a failed authentication transaction. After an Access-Accept, separately verify the authorization attributes and resulting port/VLAN state.

records.lesson_subject: Wireless mesh backhaul: root/leaf roles, CAPWAP transport, radio contention, and bridge-mode consequences
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: wireless-mesh-backhaul-root-leaf-roles-capwap-transport-radio-contention-and-bridge-mode-consequences
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Mesh replaces the wired controller path with a radio backhaul In a FortiAP wireless mesh, one AP is connected to the wired network and acts as the mesh root. Leaf APs reach the controller through a dedicated backhaul SSID rather than Ethernet. Fortinet documents that the backhaul SSID carries CAPWAP discovery, configuration, and other controller communications that a wired uplink would normally carry. The backhaul SSID is not a client SSID. Treat it as infrastructure transport, not as a second user WLAN. A leaf can associate directly to the root or to another leaf. This allows a multi-hop layout and gives a leaf an alternate parent when an AP fails, but each hop still consumes wireless airtime and reduces the capacity available to downstream clients. All mesh APs need at least one radio configured for backhaul. The root may be a FortiAP or the built-in AP of a FortiWiFi acting as controller. Dedicated versus shared radio Fortinet recommends a dedicated radio for the backhaul when the AP has sufficient radios. On a dual-radio AP, for example, one band can carry the mesh SSID while the other serves clients. This gives the backhaul a more predictable airtime budget and allows background Wi-Fi scanning in the documented dedicated-radio mode. If the same radio carries both backhaul and client SSIDs, user traffic and mesh transit contend for the same airtime. Performance is reduced, and background Wi-Fi scanning is not available in that shared-radio mode. Wireless mesh and wireless bridging are related but different deployment modes. In ordinary mesh, users associate to SSIDs on the leaf APs as they would on wired APs. In wireless bridging, the leaf AP’s Ethernet port can connect a remote wired segment; wired and wireless users behind the leaf are bridged to the LAN segment at the root. This affects where broadcast domains extend and how a remote switch or endpoint is attached. Verification and fault isolation When a leaf is offline, separate discovery from authorization and backhaul association. Confirm the root is online and authorized, the mesh SSID and security settings match, and the leaf has a radio assigned to backhaul. Check whether the leaf is associating to the expected parent and whether the backhaul radio is sharing airtime with client traffic. A leaf visible in the controller inventory proves discovery; it does not prove a stable backhaul or sufficient RF quality. When users report low throughput at distant leaves, map the parent chain and count wireless hops. Compare a dedicated-radio deployment with a shared-radio deployment, and inspect channel overlap, signal quality, and client airtime. Do not try to fix a backhaul capacity problem by changing a client SSID’s VLAN. If wireless bridging is used, verify the remote Ethernet segment and its loop/broadcast design separately. Mesh availability depends on the radio path, not merely on the AP’s management IP being reachable.

records.lesson_subject: FortiNAC 9.4 RADIUS group ingestion: Fortinet-Group-Name parsing, profile-scoped group identity, and membership reconciliation
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: fortinac-9-4-radius-group-ingestion-fortinet-group-name-parsing-profile-scoped-group-identity-and-membership-reconciliation
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: What FortiNAC 9.4 changed FortiNAC 9.4 adds support for receiving user groups from FortiAuthenticator during RADIUS authentication. The important distinction is that group membership can be carried in the RADIUS response rather than being recreated manually in FortiNAC or requiring a special FortiAuthenticator configuration change for each FortiNAC integration. The attribute is the Fortinet vendor-specific Fortinet-Group-Name , and a response can carry one or more group values. Response processing In proxy mode, FortiNAC forwards the authentication request to the selected external RADIUS server. When the Access-Accept returns, FortiNAC extracts the group names. It scopes the resulting FortiNAC group by the RADIUS proxy profile name, for example RADIUS/FAC1/Employee . If the group does not exist, FortiNAC creates a user-type group. It then finds or creates the user record and adds the user to the returned group. This namespace prevents two different RADIUS proxy profiles from silently sharing an identically named external group. Membership is reconciled, not only appended. For the same proxy-profile namespace, groups that previously existed for the user but are not present in the new returned Fortinet-Group-Name list are removed. That means the Access-Accept is the current group assertion for that RADIUS profile. If the external server stops returning a group because its policy filter changed, FortiNAC may remove the user’s membership on the next authentication. Configuration and verification On FortiAuthenticator, create or edit the user group, add the Fortinet vendor attribute and a stable group value, ensure the user is a member (directly or through the configured filter), and include that group in the applicable RADIUS policy. The group must actually be emitted in the Access-Accept; defining a local group object alone is not evidence that the attribute is sent. On FortiNAC, verify the proxy profile selected for the device/SSID, inspect the RADIUS response, and check the generated group name and user membership. If authentication succeeds but the expected Network Access Policy does not match, inspect the Access-Accept attributes first. records.lesson_subject: VPN captive portal state machine: identity-known versus agentless download, portal selection limits, and isolation release
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: vpn-captive-portal-state-machine-identity-known-versus-agentless-download-portal-selection-limits-and-isolation-release
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Portal selection is a host-state transaction FortiNAC-F’s VPN captive portal is not just a static web page. The VPN integration presents a redirect while NAC evaluates the host and decides which content page is appropriate. The VPN branch of the portal content editor includes an Index (Redirect) page, Download Page, Profile Configuration Download, Mobile Agent Download, Instructions, User Login, and Success. These are workflow states, not interchangeable HTML templates. If the VPN device provides host/user information but the endpoint does not have an agent, the Download Page is presented. If FortiNAC-F cannot find user information from the VPN device, the User Login form is used when the client first reaches the VPN context. If a host matches a supplicant policy, the Profile Configuration Download page can provide the supplicant configuration where supported. The Success page represents a host that has completed scanning and is released from isolation; it is not simply the result of a successful HTTP redirect. Multiple portal caveat When multiple captive portals are configured, Portal Policies normally determine which portal is shown during isolation. Fortinet documents a VPN-specific limitation: FortiNAC cannot properly determine the portal for VPN connections if the host does not already have an agent installed. In that agentless case, use the default portal for VPN connections. This prevents an administrator from relying on a policy selector that lacks the endpoint context it needs. Operational workflow Trace the client from VPN connection to redirect, then identify which host information arrived from the VPN device. Determine whether the endpoint is agentless and whether a user identity is available. Verify the portal content fields and the default portal association. If a scan is required, confirm the agent download/install path and the policy that releases the host from isolation. Keep the VPN portal workflow separate from wired rogue-host isolation; the state names can look similar while the identity source and redirect path differ. A portal error such as “Physical Address not found” is an identity/discovery symptom, not proof that the page template is broken. The July 2026 Community case shows this symptom for a wired isolation registration scenario. For a VPN client, first confirm what the VPN integration supplies to FortiNAC-F and whether an agent is installed. A successful VPN tunnel proves the remote user reached the VPN gateway; it does not prove NAC has a usable host record, a selected portal, or a completed scan.

records.lesson_subject: LDAP authentication cache: two-minute successful-authentication reuse, imported-user dependency, and revocation timing
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: ldap-authentication-cache-two-minute-successful-authentication-reuse-imported-user-dependency-and-revocation-timing
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Cache scope and purpose FortiAuthenticator’s documented LDAP authentication cache reduces repeated calls to a remote directory. Remote LDAP users must be imported into the FortiAuthenticator user database. After an LDAP user authenticates successfully, subsequent authentication requests from the same user within a two-minute window can succeed without another check against the remote LDAP server. This is a short successful-authentication cache, not a replacement for LDAP user import, directory synchronization, or the remote directory’s identity store. Transaction behavior On a cache miss, FortiAuthenticator must perform the remote LDAP authentication path. If that succeeds, the successful result can be reused for the same user during the documented two-minute window. Repeated requests in that interval therefore may not create a matching bind/authentication event on the LDAP server. A cache hit proves FortiAuthenticator has a recent successful result for that user; it does not prove the remote LDAP server was contacted for the current request. The performance benefit is also an operational boundary. If an account is disabled or its group membership changes in LDAP immediately after a successful authentication, do not assume every subsequent request in the next two minutes will force a fresh remote check. Treat this as a possible revocation-latency window and validate the exact behavior for the deployed release and authentication method before designing a high-risk access policy around immediate directory revocation. Verification and fault isolation Test with a controlled imported LDAP user. Record a successful authentication, then issue another authentication request within two minutes while observing both FortiAuthenticator logs and the LDAP server logs. Compare with a request after the cache window. If the first request fails, the cache is not the starting point: check LDAP server reachability, bind identity, certificate trust for LDAPS/StartTLS, search base, user import, and account state. If the first succeeds but the second succeeds during an LDAP outage, that is consistent with cache reuse; it does not prove the directory is healthy. Do not confuse the two-minute authentication cache with Remote User Sync Rule scheduling. Sync rules control importing/updating users and groups; the authentication cache controls whether a recent successful user authentication must query the remote LDAP server again. When investigating stale access, capture the exact time of the last successful authentication, the next request time, and the directory change time. Escalate only after separating cache timing from sync timing and directory reachability.

records.lesson_subject: Over-the-shoulder live recording: secret-level recording, global live stream, SSH event/video correlation, and replay lifecycle
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: over-the-shoulder-live-recording-secret-level-recording-global-live-stream-ssh-event-video-correlation-and-replay-lifecycle
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Recording is controlled at two levels FortiPAM session recording is enabled on the secret/session configuration, while Live Recording is a global setting under System Settings. Over-the-shoulder monitoring requires both: the launched secret must have Session Recording enabled, and Live Recording must be enabled globally. The live-monitoring workflow also requires Fortinet Privileged Access Agent 7.2.3 or later. Enabling the global setting alone does not turn every secret session into a recordable session. Live monitor and event correlation During a session, an administrator opens Monitoring → Active Sessions, selects the secret session, and chooses Monitor. A red video icon indicates the session is ready to be live-streamed. The monitor window displays user activity in real time, and the administrator can disconnect the active secret session from that view. This is an operational control point: live monitoring is not only post-event evidence; it can also terminate an active privileged session. For SSH sessions, FortiPAM can associate SSH command events with the session video. The secret must enable SSH service, use an SSH Filter profile, and have Session Recording enabled. In the SSH filter, only command patterns with Log enabled are linked to video. From the SSH Event log, selecting a command’s play control jumps the video to the time that command executed. Fortinet notes a one-to-two-second timestamp difference, so do not treat the event timestamp and video frame as clock-identical. Storage and replay boundary Live recording stores session video parts in an internal .chk format; the .chk file is not directly playable. FortiPAM creates a WebM representation for playback/export. The Community replay troubleshooting case documents a failure when a session does not close gracefully and the uploaded manifest is not static. That failure is different from a missing SSH command event: the recording may exist while the final manifest/video assembly is incomplete. Verification and capacity For a missing live stream, check the agent version, secret-level Session Recording, global Live Recording, active-session icon, and resource capacity. Fortinet’s guidance for multiple concurrent live sessions is eight logical CPU processors and 16 GB memory. For missing command/video links, inspect the SSH filter’s Log flag and the secret’s SSH filter assignment. For a video that never finishes loading, confirm the session closed cleanly and that the recording manifest reached a stable state; do not delete raw parts before preserving evidence. Export a playable WebM and verify the exported artifact before relying on it for an audit.

records.lesson_subject: ClickHouse event retention: ranked time policies, Hot/Warm/Cold space thresholds, archive independence, and purge boundaries
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: clickhouse-event-retention-ranked-time-policies-hot-warm-cold-space-thresholds-archive-independence-and-purge-boundaries
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Retention has two independent control planes FortiSIEM ClickHouse deployments use Online storage tiers (Hot, Warm, Cold) and may also use Archive storage. Time-based retention determines how long selected events should remain online. Space-based retention protects storage capacity when a tier approaches exhaustion. Archive retention is a separate lifecycle; an event can exist in both online and archive stores, and each has its own retention behavior. Time-based policy matching Online retention policies can scope by organization, reporting device, and event type. Policies are evaluated by rank: lower rank is evaluated first, and the first matching policy applies. After creating or changing a ClickHouse retention policy, click Apply to push it. A saved GUI row without Apply is not proof the new policy is active. Events not matched by any policy use the documented default retention value, so an unexpectedly old event may be uncovered rather than incorrectly retained by a matching policy. When the policy’s retention period expires, the event is purged from Online storage. This is different from a move from Hot to Warm or Warm to Cold, which is a capacity-tier transition and does not necessarily mean the event has expired. On non-AWS/non-GCP deployments, Cold may be sufficient as an archive tier; otherwise FortiSIEM can copy events in real time to NFS in EventDB format. AWS and GCP use their corresponding object storage options. Space-based thresholds FortiSIEM’s documented ClickHouse behavior uses free-space thresholds. If free Hot-tier disk falls below 10%, events move to Warm if configured until Hot free space exceeds 20%; without Warm, they are purged. If Warm free space falls below 10%, events move to Cold if configured until Warm exceeds 20%; without Cold, they are purged. If Cold is defined and free space drops below 10%, oldest events are purged until free space exceeds 20%. Selection is global oldest-first across retention buckets, not simply “purge the oldest event in the policy that is currently being edited.” Archive has its own space threshold. The guide describes purging oldest archive events when free archive space falls below 10 GB until it exceeds 20 GB, plus organization-based archive retention. Archive retention should not be treated as a guarantee that online events remain searchable indefinitely. Operational diagnosis If old events remain, inspect the event’s organization, reporting device, event type, policy rank, and actual retentionDays value before assuming the engine failed. The recent Community ClickHouse tip uses queries against fsiem.events_replicated to compare retentionDays with oldest/newest event dates. If events disappear earlier than expected, check space-based thresholds and whether a lower-rank policy matched first. If a policy change appears ineffective, confirm Apply was clicked. Preserve database and policy evidence before any manual cleanup; direct file deletion is not a substitute for supported retention configuration.

records.lesson_subject: Security posture tags for Secure Private Access: endpoint checks, dynamic policy source tags, and default allow-all restriction
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: security-posture-tags-for-secure-private-access-endpoint-checks-dynamic-policy-source-tags-and-default-allow-all-restriction
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Why posture tags matter In FortiSASE Secure Private Access (SPA) deployments using a FortiGate hub, the documented default is an Allow-All Private Traffic policy for agent-based remote users. That is convenient for initial connectivity but too broad when access must depend on endpoint health. Security posture tagging lets FortiSASE classify a remote user’s endpoint based on configured posture checks and then use the resulting tag as the source of a dynamic private access policy. Evaluation flow Build a posture tagging rule set for compliant endpoints and another for non-compliant endpoints. The rule sets assign tags to remote users according to the endpoint checks. A dynamic private access policy then references the tag as its source and permits or denies access to the target private application. Fortinet’s configuration workflow demonstrates a policy that allows a specific private server from compliant endpoints and a second policy that denies the same server from non-compliant endpoints. The mechanism applies to TCP, UDP, ICMP, and other private application protocols; it is not limited to web proxy traffic. The key object relationship is endpoint posture result → user tag → dynamic private access policy → FortiGate hub path → private application. A tag is an authorization input, not a route. The hub still needs a working path to the private network, and the private application still needs to listen on the expected protocol/port. If the endpoint is compliant but the private server is unreachable, do not start by changing the tag rule. Configuration and evidence Follow the documented order: create compliant posture rules, create non-compliant posture rules, create the allow policy for the compliant tag, and create the deny policy for the non-compliant tag. Test both endpoint states against the same target. The guide uses ICMP ping as a simple test, but ping only proves ICMP reachability; it does not prove a TCP application handshake, DNS resolution, or application authentication. For a user who unexpectedly has access, inspect the actual posture result and tag assigned to that user, then verify the dynamic policy source and target. For a compliant user who cannot reach an application, check the hub tunnel/path, route, FortiGate policy, and application listener after confirming the tag. Do not assume that changing a posture check instantly rewrites an already established application session; test new connections and document the release-specific reevaluation behavior. Remove or narrow the default Allow-All policy only after the restrictive tag-based policies are tested, or administrators may inadvertently create a broad access outage.

records.lesson_subject: Adaptive FEC profile selection by SLA metrics and ToS/DSCP: two-stage mapping, masks, negate thresholds, and tunnel redundancy
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: adaptive-fec-profile-selection-by-sla-metrics-and-tos-dscp-two-stage-mapping-masks-negate-thresholds-and-tunnel-redundancy
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: FEC protects a tunnel flow from loss Forward Error Correction sends redundant packets so the receiver can reconstruct some lost data without waiting for retransmission. Fortinet describes a base/redundant relationship: x redundant packets are sent for every y base packets. Adaptive FEC changes that ratio as SD-WAN SLA measurements change. With low loss, the profile can send a low redundancy ratio; as packet loss rises, the ratio can increase. This trades bandwidth for resilience, so an aggressive profile can consume capacity precisely when a link is already degraded. Two-stage mapping in FortiOS 8.0 FortiOS 8.0 adds ToS/DSCP-aware matching and negate options to adaptive FEC profiles. The first matching round evaluates packet-loss, latency, and bandwidth thresholds. The second round evaluates the packet’s ToS value and mask. This order matters: a DSCP match does not bypass the SLA threshold stage. The mask allows multiple DSCP codepoints to match a class. For example, the upper six bits of the ToS byte carry DSCP, so a value/mask pair such as 0xB8/0xFC can identify the EF codepoint while ignoring the low ECN bits. Negate options match the inverse of a threshold. Fortinet’s example explains that “negate packet-loss of 5%” matches packet loss below 5%, rather than above it. This is useful when a profile is intended for healthy paths, but it is easy to misread because the threshold number is unchanged while the comparison direction reverses. config vpn ipsec fec edit "fec-voice" config mappings edit 1 config tos edit 1 set tos 0xB8 set tos-mask 0xFC next end next end next end Use the release’s CLI reference for the complete mapping and threshold fields; the example shows the ToS selector only. The feature depends on the IPsec FEC profile and the SD-WAN SLA measurements used by that profile. It is not the same as an SD-WAN service rule selecting a WAN member based on ToS. The Community example about ToS-based SD-WAN steering also shows that an established session is not dynamically re-steered just because later packets change their ToS value. Verification and tuning Confirm the SLA health-check values, selected FEC profile, threshold match, ToS/mask match, and actual DSCP bits on the packet. Compare the observed redundancy ratio and tunnel counters before and after a controlled test. A healthy SLA probe does not prove the intended FEC mapping matched; a DSCP value in a capture does not prove the correct FEC profile was selected. If traffic receives too much redundancy, inspect negate settings and threshold ordering before increasing bandwidth. Tune with representative traffic and monitor the additional tunnel bandwidth consumed.

records.lesson_subject: FortiSwitch packet mirroring modes: local SPAN, FortiLink RSPAN VLAN 4092 and GRE-based ERSPAN
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiSwitch copies selected ingress/egress packets to a destination port (SPAN, no encapsulation), transports RSPAN copies in VLAN 4092 toward FortiGate, or encapsulates ERSPAN copies in Ethernet/IPv4/GRE to a reachable IPv4 collector; FortiLink can auto-select ISL destination and applies a policer for RSPAN/ERSPAN.
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: source-port and direction selection -> mirror engine copy -> local destination OR VLAN 4092 over ISL to FortiGate capture OR GRE/IPv4 to remote ERSPAN collector
records.failure_class: source/destination overlap; ERSPAN collector unreachable or unspecified; ISL destination conflicts; RSPAN storm-control/policer loss; unsupported model/session combination

records.remediation_path: choose a valid dedicated destination; exclude auto-selected ISL ports from source list; verify collector IPv4 reachability and FortiGate policy; confirm model/session support and policer capacity; distinguish mirror copy from forwarding path
records.question_fingerprint: RSPAN packets appear on FortiGate VLAN 4092 but not at a downstream capture host; identify the next hop and destination/transport boundary
records.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: source switch ports -> mirror engine -> three mutually distinct paths: local SPAN destination, RSPAN VLAN4092/ISL/FortiGate capture, ERSPAN GRE/IPv4 collector
records.semantic_difference: Flow export samples/exports flow records and ACLs filter packets. This lesson copies full packets through SPAN/RSPAN/ERSPAN and explains their encapsulation and destination path; neither mechanism is reused.

records.lesson_subject: FortiAP Bonjour profiles and micro-location: VLAN service advertisement with AP-group-scoped mDNS isolation

records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: service mDNS announcement on source VLAN -> Bonjour profile service/VLAN policy -> micro-location/AP group scope -> elected operating gateway -> permitted discovery on destination VLAN

records.question_fingerprint: AirPlay/printer discovery crosses floors despite VLAN mapping; determine whether micro-location and AP group scoping are correctly applied
records.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: two AP groups representing separate locations, each with an elected Bonjour gateway; source VLAN -> service policy -> destination VLAN, with no cross-location mDNS path

records.lesson_subject: FortiNAC 9.4 RADIUS Activity: 802.1X/MAB pass-fail telemetry and failed-authentication export

records.lesson_subject: FortiNAC-F Mist Service Connector: API-based site discovery, virtual-controller inventory and manual migration from CloudAPITool
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiNAC-F Service Connector uses the Mist Device Management API with API domain, port 443, organization ID and full-permission token; selected sites create a virtual controller and AP inventory on the next poll; optional switch discovery requires SNMP and CLI credentials; RADIUS, L2/L3 polling and CoA provide visibility/enforcement; legacy CloudAPITool inventory is not automatically migrated.

records.failure_class: wrong regional API domain/token/organization ID; missing SNMP+CLI credentials; polling exceeds 5000 API calls/hour; old CloudAPITool devices remain; RADIUS source IP/shared secret/CoA timestamp mismatch

records.lesson_subject: FortiAuthenticator EAP-TEAP: chained machine and user authentication inside one RADIUS session
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiAuthenticator 8.0.2 RADIUS supports TEAP, chaining machine and user authentication in one session; both must succeed; each inner authentication can use EAP-MSCHAPv2 or EAP-TLS; Auth Profiles bind authentication type, identity sources and factors to a RADIUS policy; client groups can scope policy selection.
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: supplicant -> AP/switch authenticator -> RADIUS -> TEAP outer tunnel -> machine inner authentication -> user inner authentication -> both successful -> Access-Accept
records.failure_class: machine phase fails; user phase fails; incompatible inner EAP method; server/client certificate trust failure; wrong authentication profile or RADIUS client group
records.evidence_pattern: RADIUS transaction shows TEAP and phase outcome; Authentication > RADIUS Service > Auth Profiles; policy profile binding; client group membership; certificate validity and trust; separate machine/user test results
records.remediation_path: create an Auth Profile with intended identity sources/factors; bind it to the correct RADIUS policy and client group; verify both inner methods independently; validate certificate trust for EAP-TLS; require both machine and user success
records.question_fingerprint: Machine authentication succeeds but the user phase fails; determine whether the chained TEAP session should be accepted and which profile evidence to inspect
records.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: endpoint -> AP/switch -> FortiAuthenticator RADIUS -> TEAP tunnel containing machine-auth and user-auth stages -> AND gate -> Access-Accept/Reject
records.semantic_difference: EAP-TTLS two-factor and SmartConnect EAP-TLS binding do not chain machine and user identity inside a single TEAP transaction. This lesson teaches TEAP's two-stage AND condition and Auth Profile binding.

records.lesson_subject: FortiPAM 1.9 launcher privilege: independent USER/SYSTEM execution contexts for application and init/clean commands
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiPAM 1.9 launcher Privilege selects four combinations: launch secret under USER or SYSTEM and run init/clean commands under USER or SYSTEM; FortiClient 8.0+ honors the flag, while FortiClient 7.x uses legacy hardcoded behavior (SSMS as SYSTEM, other processes as USER).
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: secret authorization -> FortiClient launcher receives privilege flag -> init command runs under selected identity -> target application process starts under selected identity -> clean command runs under selected identity -> session audit/recording
records.failure_class: application requires SYSTEM but runs as USER; init/clean requires SYSTEM but app requires USER; unsupported FortiClient version silently follows legacy mapping
records.evidence_pattern: Secret Settings > Launchers Privilege selection; FortiClient version; Task Manager Details User name for process; init/clean command result and launcher logs
records.remediation_path: select the correct one of four privilege combinations; standardize on FortiClient 8.0+ where per-launcher control is required; verify process owner in Task Manager and test init/clean independently
records.question_fingerprint: An application launches only when elevated but its initialization script needs the user's profile; choose the privilege combination that separates the two contexts
records.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiPAM secret/launcher policy -> FortiClient -> split USER/SYSTEM execution selectors -> init command, target application and clean command

records.lesson_subject: FortiSIEM Linux Agent service supervision: HTTPS registration/event flow and systemd restart behavior after SIGSEGV
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiSIEM Linux Agent registers outbound over HTTPS to the Supervisor, periodically receives monitoring-template updates, and forwards events to Collectors; systemd service state controls process restart, and RemainAfterExit=yes can leave a crashed SIGSEGV process reported active instead of restarted.
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: systemd starts phLinuxAgent -> agent HTTPS registration to Supervisor -> monitoring-template update -> event forwarding to Collector; SIGSEGV exit -> systemd unit state evaluation -> restart only if unit semantics permit
records.failure_class: agent process exits with signal 11 but systemd RemainAfterExit=yes masks the stopped process and prevents automatic restart
records.evidence_pattern: systemctl status fortisiem-linux-agent.service; journalctl/dmesg SIGSEGV; service unit RemainAfterExit; Supervisor registration status; Collector event freshness; rsyslog/package prerequisites
records.remediation_path: set RemainAfterExit=no in the service unit as documented in the scenario; systemctl daemon-reload; restart the service; separately investigate the underlying segmentation fault and verify Supervisor/Collector connectivity
records.question_fingerprint: Linux Agent logs SIGSEGV but systemd still reports the unit active; identify the unit directive that prevents restart
records.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Linux host systemd supervisor -> phLinuxAgent -> HTTPS Supervisor registration/template channel -> Collector event channel; crash path loops through systemd restart decision
records.semantic_difference: Prior lessons covered Windows endpoint FIM, rule execution and manager-to-manager control. This lesson covers Linux agent process supervision, systemd state semantics and crash recovery.

records.lesson_subject: FortiSASE pre-logon connectivity: machine-certificate tunnel to Active Directory before first Windows domain login
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Pre-logon connectivity establishes a machine-certificate-authenticated tunnel at Windows boot so a never-logged-in domain-joined endpoint can reach AD; after interactive login the pre-logon tunnel disconnects, and the endpoint transitions to user tunnel/autoconnect; subsequent logins can use cached AD credentials. SAML password persistence requires IdP persistent sessions; OAuth tunnel support is limited to Entra ID/Windows/SSL.
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Windows boot -> FortiClient pre-logon profile -> machine certificate authentication -> gateway tunnel -> AD domain controller reachability -> first interactive domain login -> pre-logon disconnect -> user tunnel autoconnect -> cached credentials for later logins
records.failure_class: missing/expired machine certificate; unsupported FortiClient profile/version; AD not reachable through pre-logon tunnel; confusion between machine pre-logon and user tunnel; IdP does not support persistent SAML sessions
records.evidence_pattern: pre-logon tunnel establishment before user sign-in; machine certificate chain; FortiClient logs; AD DC reachability; tunnel disconnect after login; subsequent cached login; IdP persistent-session capability
records.remediation_path: stage supported FortiClient and machine certificates before device shipment; validate gateway and AD routes while pre-logon is active; confirm the tunnel transitions after user login; configure OAuth/SAML persistence only within documented platform limits
records.question_fingerprint: A new domain-joined laptop cannot perform its first interactive login off-network because no cached credentials exist; select the correct machine-authenticated pre-logon path
records.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: booted Windows endpoint -> machine certificate -> temporary pre-logon tunnel -> AD DC -> user login -> pre-logon teardown -> user-authenticated FortiSASE tunnel

records.lesson_subject: Secure SD-WAN Fabric Overlay Orchestrator IPAM integration: deterministic hub/spoke loopback and tunnel address allocation

records.lesson_subject: Transparent conditional DNS forwarding: zone-matched interception, local answers, and site-local resolver selection
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: DNS proxy parses configured dns-database zones, matches QNAME/domain filters, checks local dns-entry data, then selects zone-specific forwarder or original destination; the database is attached to a DNS filter profile and only works on proxy-based firewall policies.
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Client sends DNS to its configured resolver; FortiGate transparently intercepts the query in a proxy inspection policy; matching zone chooses local answer or forwarder; unmatched names continue to original destination; response returns to client.
records.failure_class: Wrong authoritative flag, unmatched zone, missing DNS-filter policy binding, flow-mode policy, unreachable forwarder, wrong source IP across VPN, or unsupported low-memory model.
records.evidence_pattern: nslookup returns configured local A record for office.microsoft.com, local resolver answer for another matching name, and central resolver answer for unmatched facebook.com; packet capture shows client-to-FortiGate and FortiGate-to-forwarder transactions.
records.remediation_path: Enable DNS Database feature visibility; define zone and local entries; disable authoritative when upstream fallback is intended; set forwarder and source-ip/source-ip6; attach zone to DNS filter profile; apply it to proxy-based policy; verify route, source address, and RAM/model support.
records.question_fingerprint: Given local SaaS DNS answers differ from central answers, identify the domain-match decision and distinguish local-record, zone-forwarder, and unmatched-query paths.
records.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Three-branch DNS decision graph: client query into FortiGate DNS proxy, QNAME match diamond, then local answer, zone forwarder, or original resolver; responses converge to client.

records.lesson_subject: Per-policy workspace locking: granular concurrent-edit isolation and policy-sequence ownership
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Workspace mode plus per-policy-lock lets an administrator lock a single policy rather than an entire package or ADOM; policies used by Policy Blocks cannot be individually locked; adding/reordering multiple policies creates a separate sequence lock.
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Administrator selects ADOM and package, acquires policy lock, edits and saves; competing administrators see lock owner/color and cannot modify that policy; sequence lock serializes insert/reorder operations and disappears after save.
records.failure_class: Workspace/per-policy locking disabled, policy belongs to a Policy Block, stale lock ownership, or sequence lock blocks policy insertion/reordering.
records.evidence_pattern: Green padlock identifies the current administrator's lock; red padlock identifies another administrator's lock; hover tooltip exposes owner and timestamp; sequence-lock banner appears when multiple policies are added.
records.remediation_path: Enable Workspace mode and Per-Policy Lock in System Settings > Advanced > Workspace or set config system global per-policy-lock enable; verify correct ADOM/package; use package/ADOM lock for Policy Block members; complete save and release lock before handoff.
records.question_fingerprint: Distinguish a single-policy edit lock from the sequence lock required for ordering changes and from whole-package/ADOM locks.
records.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Two-admin concurrency swimlane around one shared policy package, with single-policy lock and separate sequence-lock gate on insert/reorder.

records.lesson_subject: Cloud archive offload with Storage Fabric Connectors: connector identity, CA trust, license gate, and remote-path binding
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiAnalyzer Device Log Settings binds an enabled Fabric storage connector and remote bucket/container path to log upload; a valid Storage Connector Service license and cloud-provider CA chain are prerequisites for S3, Azure Blob, or Google storage.
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Create provider connector with region and credential material; import provider CA certificates; enable Upload logs to cloud storage; choose connector and remote path; FortiAnalyzer uploads log files to the configured cloud bucket/container.
records.failure_class: Missing storage-service entitlement, disabled connector, incorrect provider region or credentials, wrong bucket/container path, missing CA chain, or outbound TLS/network failure.
records.evidence_pattern: License Information shows entitlement; Fabric Connectors shows connector enabled; Device Log Settings shows selected connector and remote path; provider-side object listing/audit logs confirm upload; local Analytics and Archive availability must be checked separately.
records.remediation_path: Validate Storage Connector Service license; create the correct S3/Azure Blob/Google connector; verify region and credential scope; import provider CA certificates; enable upload and set exact remote path; test outbound DNS/TLS and confirm provider-side objects.
records.question_fingerprint: Identify which dependency explains a cloud upload failure when local log ingestion continues: connector entitlement, remote path, or CA trust.
records.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiAnalyzer archive pipeline branching from local log storage through a license/connector/CA gate to cloud object storage, with analytics database shown as a separate local path.

records.lesson_subject: FortiLink-managed dual-signed FortiSwitchOS image verification: controller validation and pre-upgrade trust evidence
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiOS 7.6.5 switch controller adds OS image signature verification for dual-signed FortiSwitchOS images; FortiSwitchOS GUI also exposes image integrity verification, with model/BIOS support determining whether verification is available.
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Administrator selects an image for a managed switch; controller and switch firmware-support path validate image signature/integrity before installation; unsupported BIOS or failed signature produces explicit warning rather than a clean verified state.
records.failure_class: Unverified or invalid image signature, BIOS without signature-verification support, unsupported model/image combination, or assuming a successful file transfer equals trusted firmware.
records.evidence_pattern: GUI warning 'Firmware failed signature validation', 'Unverified Image Detected', or red warning triangle; release/model feature matrix establishes whether BIOS and hardware support verification.
records.remediation_path: Use an official Fortinet image for the exact model and supported release; verify model/feature matrix and BIOS capability; stop on signature warnings; remediate firmware/BIOS compatibility through supported upgrade guidance rather than bypassing verification.
records.question_fingerprint: Differentiate image upload success from signature validation and identify the correct response to a BIOS-capability warning.
records.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiManager/FortiGate controller to FortiLink switch upgrade flow with image intake, signature-verification gate, BIOS capability check, and install/stop branches.

records.lesson_subject: Wi-Fi 7 Multi-Link Operation: MLD link association, WPA3 prerequisites, radio-profile binding, and standalone behavior
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiAP-K MLO exposes one multi-link device across supported 2.4/5/6-GHz radios; requires FAP 7.6.3+, supported model/radio, WPA3-SAE with H2E-only or WPA3 Enterprise Only; standalone mode on supported K models requires FAP 7.6.5+, bridge mode and local authentication.
